Build the "All settings" panel that Kenneth approved on 2026-10-20, in JusPrin's Agent pane (repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin).

## The design (source of truth)
The Claude canvas artifact "JusPrin v2", https://claude.ai/artifact/VCEppdwfT7v32W4beUxL1v, page "Current Setup Card". Read these four boards with the Artifact tool (action "read", path "project/<file>"):
- setup-card-all-settings-entry.dc.html: the expanded setup card with an "All settings" link (Button/Link) at the bottom, under the "N changes from preset" disclosure.
- setup-card-all-settings-project.dc.html: the panel at whole-project scope.
- setup-card-all-settings-object.dc.html: the panel scoped to one object, with the Changed filter on.
- setup-card-all-settings-filaments.dc.html: the Filament group with three slots side by side.
The Design System artifact, https://claude.ai/artifact/3zgiix8rAw3rXextQnR5UL, has the components the boards reuse: Select, SegmentedControl, FieldSearch, Swatch, Button/Link and Button/Icon. Figma is retired; don't cite or change it.

## What the panel is
- It takes the Agent pane's place, with a back button (to the chat) and the title "All settings". It opens from the setup card's "All settings" link.
- Top controls:
  - "Showing" Select: Whole project, each plate, each object. It follows the selection in the 3D view.
  - A FieldSearch "Search settings".
  - A SegmentedControl All / Changed.
- Whole project:
  - A "presets in use" box: printer (with nozzle), filament per slot (swatch + name), process preset with "N changes from the preset", and any plate setting of its own (e.g. "Plate 1 · Textured PEI · Bed type set on this plate").
  - A note naming objects that have settings of their own.
  - Then collapsible groups in OrcaSlicer's own categories: Quality, Strength, Speed, Support, Others, Filament, Printer. Each group header shows a summary on the right ("3 changed", "from the preset").
  - A row is name + value. A changed value is bold, with "Preset: <value>" under it. Overrides elsewhere are noted under the row ("Mounting tabs: 6").
- One object (or part/modifier/height range): the object's own settings, each with what it overrides ("Mounting tabs · 2 regions · project: 4") and an action ("Use project value", or "Remove" for support blockers). Groups it doesn't change say "same as project".
- Filaments: with 2 or 3 slots, the Filament group shows one column per slot (swatch, slot, material) for nozzle and first-layer temperature, bed temperature for the plate's bed type, fan speed, flow ratio and retraction. A value inherited from the printer reads "printer" (muted). A filament's own override is bold, with a note. With more than 3 slots, ask Kenneth (the design suggests a slot picker instead of columns).

## OrcaSlicer's real structure (the design depends on it)
- Printer, filament (one preset per slot) and process presets are separate, not one inheritance chain.
- A filament overrides only a few printer settings (its "setting overrides": retraction, z-hop, wipe and similar; see filament_retraction_length etc. in src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp).
- A plate has only a few settings of its own (bed type, print sequence, first-layer filament order, spiral vase; src/slic3r/GUI/PlateSettingsDialog.cpp).
- Objects, parts, modifiers and height ranges override process settings.
Verify each against the code before relying on it, and attribute behaviour correctly (AGENTS.md "Upstream vs. fork attribution").

## Where things are
- The setup card: src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/SetupCard.tsx, rendered once in App.tsx. The page bundles build through CMake; see agent-docs/jusprin/README.md and the memory note on web bundles.
- Settings data: the Agent already reads settings through host tools (settings_get, settings_search, settings_preview_patch in the JusPrin MCP/tool registry under src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/). Reuse that host code for the panel's data rather than writing a second reader. The page talks to the host through the bridge (AgentUI/src/bridge/protocol.ts). Add a capability, not a protocol version bump.
- Editing from the panel ("Use project value", "Remove") changes settings. Discuss with Kenneth whether the first version is read-only plus those two actions, or read-only only.

## Rules
- Read agent-docs/jusprin/README.md, agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md ("Writing UI code"; every size and colour comes from resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json) and agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md before touching files outside src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/.
- Work in your own new worktree off jusprin-newui. Never reuse another session's worktree. The composer work is on claude/composer-redesign (uncommitted changes there belong to another session).
- Fail-first for every new guard test. Restore from a saved copy, never `git checkout`.
- No live AI model calls without Kenneth approving a specific batch.
- Commit only when Kenneth asks.
- The setup card's left "live" stripe (.current-setup--live) is being reviewed separately. Leave it alone.
- Before building, list the open questions for Kenneth (editing scope, more than 3 slots, how plates appear in "Showing") and ask them together.
I'll start by checking which branch this worktree is cut from, reading the project docs the brief names, and reading the four design boards. Then I'll ask Kenneth the open questions before building.

---
name: jusprin-worktree-build
description: How to configure a JusPrin worktree build reusing existing deps; BUILD_TESTS=ON needed for tests
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference

A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:

```
cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
```

CMAKE BINARY (2026-09-29): configure with `/Applications/CMake.app/Contents/bin/cmake` (put it first on PATH). Homebrew's cmake 4.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin fails with "Could NOT find Eigen3 (missing: EIGEN3_VERSION_OK) (Required is at least version 5.0.1)", and a failed configure poisons the cache: `rm -rf build` before retrying.

The two `CMAKE_AR`/`CMAKE_RANLIB` flags are required on a FRESH build dir:
without them Apple's ar is used and liblibslic3r_gui.a (>4 GiB in
RelWithDebInfo) fails to archive. They only work at first configure, not on
reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].

FRESH WORKTREE TRAP (2026-09-18): building only `shell_integration_harness`
does not build the web pages. Also build `--target jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs`
(needs node on PATH: /Users/kenneth/.nvm/versions/node/v24.13.0/bin). Without
them resources/jusprin/{home,agent}/index.html are missing, no web views are
created, and the harness silently tests something else (printer panel starts
shown; web-view crashes vanish).

`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

CWD TRAP (cost real time once): the harness resets the Bash cwd to the main
repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a
stale lib without recompiling a changed .cpp in that lib — build the app target
(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with
`grep -c '<file>.cpp.o' build.log`. Editing tools (Edit/Write) use absolute
paths so source edits land correctly regardless of cwd.

STALE PROMPT TRAP (2026-09-23): `--target shell_integration_harness` does NOT
rebuild the web pages, so a harness run after an edit to AgentUI (for example
printerInstructions.ts) loads the old bundle. Six --printer-live runs were
wasted this way. After any page edit, build `jusprin_web` explicitly and check
the new text is in resources/jusprin/agent/index.html before running live.

DISK (2026-10-10): building with `--config Release` instead of RelWithDebInfo made a fresh worktree build dir 859 MB instead of ~14 GB, needed no llvm-ar relink, and the shell harness ran normally from `tests/shell/Release/`. Use it when the disk is nearly full (it was at 99%) and no debugger is needed. With other sessions building, a fresh build took far longer than usual (machine load 30 to 85).

Phase 2 (read-only deterministic Agent) implemented on `jusprin-newui` on 2026-08-30.

- Native bridge: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/` — `AgentHost` (GUI-free coordinator, owns the authoritative conversation; streaming advances only via `pump_stream()`), `DeterministicMockAgent` (`/fail`, `/flaky`, `/slow` scenarios), `AgentWebView` (wx transport + internal-error surface).
- React page: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/` (npm package). `npm run build` writes the committed single-file bundle `resources/jusprin/agent/index.html`; the C++ build never needs Node. Rebuild + recommit the bundle whenever AgentUI changes.
- Shared protocol source: `resources/jusprin/agent/protocol.json` — both `tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp` and the vitest suite assert their constants against it. Bump the version there and in `AgentProtocol.hpp`/`protocol.ts` together.
- Workspace contract gained `WorkspaceSetup` (project/printer/filament) and per-plate `sliced`; adding fields to `WorkspacePlate` breaks brace-initializers in `tests/workspace/test_workspace_contract.cpp`.

## Governing decisions

- JusPrin is an AI-piloted 3D-printing product built on OrcaSlicer, not a replacement slicing engine.
- OrcaSlicer's C++ model, slicing pipeline, viewport, geometry operations, project serialization, and undo stack remain authoritative.

111	
112	Design for a dense, native, high-DPI desktop application on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Use device-independent pixels (DIP), not physical pixels. Verify 100%, 150%, and 200% scaling.
113	
114	- Spacing scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, and 48 DIP.
115	- The radius scale carries the design system's names (`dimension.radius`):
116	  - `small`, 4 DIP: standard controls (secondary and icon buttons, fields, the segmented control), matching OrcaSlicer's own controls.
117	  - `medium`, 8 DIP: containers (cards, popovers, chat bubbles) and the primary button, the one branded action.
118	  - `large`, 12 DIP: sheets, large dialogs and window actions.
119	  - `chip`, 4 DIP: the printer and filament chip in the header.
120	  - `full`, 10 DIP: capsule ends of status chips and progress tracks up to 20 DIP tall.

176	only if the code goes through the token file in the first place.

178	1. **Never type a color, radius, font, or control size.** Every one comes
179	   from `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json`. Native code reads it
180	   through `ShellTheme`: `palette(dark)` for color, `metrics()` for radii,
181	   spacing, and per-component sizes, `font(role)` for type. A stock
182	   `wxStaticText`, `wxTextCtrl`, or OrcaSlicer `Button` is

1	# Fork stewardship
2	
3	**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.
4	
5	JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.
6	
7	One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**
8	
9	- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
10	- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
11	- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.
12	
13	Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.
14	
15	## The ten principles
16	
17	### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much
18	
19	**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.
20	
21	**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.
22	
23	**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?
24	
25	**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.
26	
27	### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge
28	
29	**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.
30	
31	**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.
32	
33	**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?
34	
35	**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.
36	
37	### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it
38	
39	**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.
40	
41	**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.
42	
43	**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?
44	
45	**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.
46	
47	### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism
48	
49	**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.
50	
51	**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.
52	
53	**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?
54	
55	**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.
56	
57	### 5. One seam beats many touch points
58	
59	**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.
60	
61	**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.
62	
63	**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?
64	
65	**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.
66	
67	### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict
68	
69	**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.
70	
71	**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.
72	
73	**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.
74	
75	**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.
76	
77	### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly
78	
79	**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.
80	
81	**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.
82	
83	**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?
84	
85	**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.
86	
87	### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went
88	
89	**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.
90	
91	**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.
92	
93	**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?
94	
95	**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.
96	
97	### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it
98	
99	**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.
100	
101	**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.
102	
103	**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?
104	
105	**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
106	
107	### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit
108	
109	**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.
110	
111	**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. Merging upstream in makes the conflict surface the entire divergence between the release branch and upstream's development line — none of it ours. Rebasing only our commits discards that inherited history by taking upstream's version of every file we never touched.
112	
113	**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?
114	
115	**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.
116	
117	## Before you finish
118	
119	A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:
120	
121	1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.
122	
123	   ```bash
124	   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
125	   ```
126	
127	   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.
128	
129	2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.
130	
131	3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
132	
133	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.
134	
135	## This fork's terrain
136	
137	Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.
138	
139	`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.
140	
141	Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.
142	
143	`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
144	upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
145	updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
146	or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
147	error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
148	strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
149	controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
150	print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
151	into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
152	19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
153	needed edits across eight upstream files.
154	
155	The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
156	after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
157	Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
158	correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
159	Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
160	fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
161	Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
162	no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
163	replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
164	addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
165	`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
166	on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
167	must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.
168	
169	Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
170	screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
171	availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
172	selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
173	Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
174	page, silently.
175	
176	Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
177	function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
178	sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
179	`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
180	and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
181	without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
182	owned by Plater's event handler.
183	
184	Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

# JusPrin Agent UI

The local React/TypeScript application that renders the Agent conversation
pane inside `wxWebView`. It talks to OrcaSlicer exclusively through the
versioned `jusprin-agent-bridge` JSON protocol whose shared source of truth is
`resources/jusprin/agent/protocol.json`; the native side lives in
`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/`.

The page renders native state and submits typed requests. It never owns an
editable copy of the project or conversation: the native `AgentHost` is
authoritative, and every reload re-runs the handshake and reconstructs the
page from the host's `state` message.

## Building

CMake builds this page whenever an input changes (`npm ci` from the lockfile, then `npm run build`). The output is `resources/jusprin/agent/index.html`; it is generated, not committed. Node/npm is required unless you configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply that file yourself.

```bash
cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target jusprin_web
```

The bundle must stay a single self-contained file (`vite-plugin-singlefile`):
WKWebView does not reliably load `file:` subresources.

To point the running app at a Vite dev server instead of the packaged file (hot
module reload):

```bash
cd src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI && npm run dev
JUSPRIN_AGENT_DEV_URL=http://localhost:5173 ./build/arm64/src/OrcaSlicer.app/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer
```

Adjust the binary path for your build tree and platform. The environment
variable is read once at construction; there is no settings UI for it.

## Testing

```bash
npm test        # vitest: protocol, bridge client, reducer, and DOM interaction tests
```

The deterministic conversation scenarios (`/fail`, `/flaky`, `/slow`) are
implemented natively in `DeterministicMockAgent.cpp` and asserted by
`tests/agent/test_agent_bridge.cpp`; the tests here exercise the page against
a scripted mock host playing the same protocol.

### State matrices

`src/visual/` holds one state input per state on the Figma page **Agent UI ·
States & Components**: runtime and header states, chat
list, composer, messages, manufacturing history, the earlier-chat notice, and
the printer chat. Each is rendered by the production components, or by the
real `App` against a scripted host, so a state is covered only if real inputs
can produce it. `npm test` asserts every one renders; with an output path the
same test writes a review page of all of them at the 429 and 320 DIP dock
widths in both appearances:

```bash
PREVIEW_OUT=/tmp/agent-ui-states.html npx vitest run AgentUiStateMatrix
```

Open the page with `?show=<case>,<case>&mode=dark&dock=320` to narrow it to
the states being compared with a Figma node. The page proves rendering only;
look at the running app as well (`tests/shell`'s capture modes write PNGs of
the real WebView).

## Design

`tokens.ts` imports `resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json` at build time
and writes it onto the root element as custom properties: `--<group>-<name>`
for the semantic colors of the appearance the host reports, and, once at
startup, `--radius-<name>` for each radius plus `--font-<role>` holding the
complete `font` shorthand of each type role and `--font-code` for the one
monospace role, used only for code, keys, paths and IDs. `styles.css` may use only those variables for
color, radius, and type, and only the spacing scale (4 through 48) for
padding, margin, and gap; `styles.test.ts` reads the stylesheet from disk and
fails on any literal outside that contract, naming the offending line.

The one reader underneath every tool is the `IWorkspace` interface, implemented by `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter`, plus a few header-only helpers. That reader only covers four scopes (process, object, filament preset, printer preset).

All paths below are relative to `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/sharp-snyder-2d935e`.

## 1. The six tools

**Where they live**
- **Schemas:** `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp`, built in one `definitions{...}` vector.
- **Dispatch:** `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute()` in `Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`, branching on `ToolHandler::*`.
- **JSON shaping:** `Agent/ToolResults.cpp`.
- **MCP:** uses the same coordinator. `Mcp/McpRuntime.cpp:71` calls `m_coordinator.submit(...)`.

**Common pieces**
- **Scope enum** (`ToolRegistry.cpp:946`): `"process" | "object" | "filament" | "printer"`.
- **`target`** (`:950`): `{objectId?, preset?}`. Leave it out for process; object takes `objectId`; filament and printer take the preset's exact name.
- **Parsing:** `settings_target()` at `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:318-340` maps the strings to `Workspace::SettingsScope`.
- **Every settings result also carries** `scope, presetName, sessionId, revision, truncated` (`settings_output` at `ToolRegistry.cpp:926-934`, filled by `settings_context` at `ToolResults.cpp:40-45`).

**The tools**

| Tool | Schema | Handler | Workspace call | JSON builder |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `settings_search` | `ToolRegistry.cpp:1039-1045` | `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:1891-1914` | `search_settings(SettingsQuery)` | `settings_search_result`, `ToolResults.cpp:82-104` |
| `settings_get` | `:1046-1055` | `:1916-1932` | `read_settings(keys, target)` | `settings_read_result`, `:106-126` |
| `settings_preview_patch` | `:1056-1061` | `:1934-1950` | `preview_settings(SettingsPatch)` | `settings_preview_result`, `:128-140` |
| `settings_apply_patch` | `:1062-1070` | preflight `:747-770`, run `:1952-1983` | `apply_settings(patch, expected, applied)` | `settings_apply_result`, `:142-162` |
| `presets_list` | `:1396-1409` | `:1678-1692` | `list_presets(PresetQuery)` | `presets_list_result`, `:898-909` |
| `workspace_inspect` | `:1484-1512` | `:956-1003` | `snapshot()`, plus product state | `workspace_inspection`, `:752-795`, plus section builders |

**Inputs and outputs**
- **`settings_search`**
  - In: `{scope, target?, query, limit 1..25, cursor, writable, changedOnly}`. `scope` and `query` are required.
  - Out: `{items:[{key, type, label, category, description, unit, min?, max?, enumValues[], enumLabels[], writable, truncated}], nextCursor}`.
  - The cursor format is `"offset:N"`.
- **`settings_get`**
  - In: `{scope, target?, keys[1..32]}`.
  - Out: `{items:[{key, value, type, label, unit, differsFromPreset, differsFromSystem, writable, overridden?}], unknownKeys:[issue]}`.
  - `value` is Orca's `ConfigOption::serialize()` string.
  - `get` returns no `category`, enum options or preset value; only `search` returns those definition fields.
  - `overridden` appears only for object scope.
- **`settings_preview_patch`**
  - In: `{scope, target?, changes:{key: string|number|bool} (1..32), persistAs?}`.
  - Out: `{valid, changes:[{key, before, after}], dependencies:[...], issues:[issue], warnings:[issue]}`.
  - Issue shape: `{key, code, message, allowed[], suggestions[], min?, max?, truncated}`.
- **`settings_apply_patch`**
  - In: the preview inputs plus `expectedSessionId, expectedRevision`.
  - Out: `{applied, changes, normalized[], savedAs, presetDirty, projectUndo}`. `projectUndo` is true only for object scope.

- **`presets_list`**

**How scope works**

`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2725-2756` decides which config is read:
- **Process:** the selected print preset's edited copy.
- **Object:** the same process config with `ModelObject::config` layered on top. Overridable keys are `PrintRegionConfig` or `PrintObjectConfig` options (`OrcaSettingDefinitions.hpp:53-58`).
- **Filament or printer:** the preset looked up by name. If it is the selected one, its edited copy is read; otherwise it is read as saved.
- **Filament slots:** there is no slot index in this API. The slot list is `preset_bundle->filament_presets` (see `filament_slot()` at `:2801`).
- **Not supported by any settings tool:** plate, part, modifier, layer range.

```cpp
if (owner.selected) {
    dirty  = owner.collection->current_dirty_options();
    system = owner.collection->current_different_from_parent_options();
} else if (const Preset* base = owner.collection->get_preset_base(*owner.preset); ...)
```
